demo_steps.title: Original three-panel comparison
demo_steps.narration: The default view reproduces the textbook composition: a), b), and c) appear simultaneously from left to right. The same idea is shown in increasing input dimension.

demo_steps.title: a) One input dimension
demo_steps.narration: In 1D, the equation w_1 x_1 + b = 0 has a zero set that is just a point on the x_1 line. The origin dot marks that threshold crossing.

demo_steps.title: b) Two input dimensions
demo_steps.narration: In 2D, each neuron's zero set becomes a line. The teal vertical line and orange horizontal line each split the x_1-x_2 plane into two half-spaces.

demo_steps.title: c) Three input dimensions
demo_steps.narration: In 3D, the boundaries become planes. The gray, teal, and orange rectangular sheets show coordinate-aligned hyperplanes slicing the x_1-x_2-x_3 input space.

demo_steps.title: Dimension rule
demo_steps.narration: Returning to all panels makes the pattern explicit: increasing the input dimension from 1 to 2 to 3 turns the boundary from a point to a line to a plane.

plan.geometry_notes: Overall layout: three separate panels on one horizontal row, occupying roughly equal widths. Use a clean white background and black math-style labels. Do not show hidden-pattern labels, class labels, sign badges, equation text, normal arrows, dashed guides, legends, draggable input points, or half-space shading by default. Approximate panel centers in world/screen layout: panel a at x=-5.5, panel b at x=0, panel c at x=5.7, all centered vertically near y=0. Panel labels a), b), c) sit above each panel, slightly left of each panel's main geometry, in black. Panel a: horizontal x_1 axis length about 3.6 units, from -1.8 to +1.8 within the panel, y=0; draw a small black dot radius about 0.07 at the center/origin. Axis stroke black #111111, label x_1 just beyond the positive right end. Panel b: x_1 and x_2 axes each span about -1.7 to +1.7, crossing at the origin; x_1 exactly horizontal and x_2 exactly vertical. The teal hyperplane is a vertical thick line centered on x_1=0, from y=-1.45 to +1.45, color #7fc8c3 or #8ccfca, opacity 0.9, stroke/strip width about 0.10. The orange hyperplane is a horizontal thick line centered on x_2=0, from x=-1.45 to +1.45, color #c97955 or #d1815f, opacity 0.9, same thickness as teal. The black origin dot remains visible on top of the colored crossing. Panel c must match the source orientation: screen x_1 is horizontal to the right, screen x_2 is vertical upward, and screen x_3 slants down-left at roughly 35 to 45 degrees below the negative horizontal direction. Use an axonometric basis for panel c approximately e1=(1,0), e2=(0,1), e3=(-0.72,-0.45) in screen units. The three 3D rectangles should be larger and more source-like than thin slices: gray plane is a vertical frontal rectangle spanning x_1 by x_2 with size about 2.1 wide × 1.8 high, color #cfd5d6, opacity 0.75; its front face edges remain horizontal/vertical. Teal plane is a vertical slanted rectangle spanning x_3 by x_2, attached to the left side/shared vertical edge of the gray plane and receding down-left, size about 1.55 along x_3 × 1.8 along x_2, color #74c6c1, opacity 0.8. Orange plane is a horizontal slanted rectangle spanning x_1 by x_3, attached along the lower horizontal edge of the gray plane and receding down-left, size about 2.1 along x_1 × 1.55 along x_3, color #d1815f, opacity 0.82. All three panel c planes should have comparable visual extents and meet cleanly at the coordinate triad; draw subtle darker edges only where needed to read the planar geometry. The origin for panel c is the common corner/axis intersection where x_1, x_2, and x_3 begin; x_1 points right along the lower/front edge, x_2 points up along the vertical edge, and x_3 points down-left along the receding edge. Axis labels are black, placed just outside arrow tips. Mathematical concept: each neuron boundary is the zero set w^T x + b = 0; for the source-like static geometry use b=0 and coordinate-aligned examples: in 1D x_1=0 is a point, in 2D x_1=0 and x_2=0 are lines, in 3D x_1=0, x_2=0, and x_3=0 are planes.
plan.notes: Render as a static simultaneous multipanel composition by default. Use independent grouped coordinate systems for each panel rather than one shared 3D scene, so panel a and b remain flat and panel c keeps the required axonometric basis. The layoutMode toggle should only zoom/focus or fade non-focused panels; it must not replace the default all-panels composition. conceptLabels=false must recreate the clean source figure with only panel labels, axis labels, axes, dot, lines, and planes. If conceptLabels=true, add small unobtrusive labels such as 'point', 'line', and 'plane' near the corresponding boundaries, preferably outside the main geometry. Hover tooltips should be transient UI overlays, not persistent scene geometry. Use transparent double-sided materials for the colored planes, but avoid extra lighting effects that make them look like unrelated solids; flat shaded pastel rectangles are closest to the source.

authoredPrompt: This figure illustrates how individual neurons in a shallow neural network define hyperplane decision boundaries in input spaces of increasing dimension, across three side-by-side panels labeled a), b), and c). Panel a) shows a one-dimensional input space with a horizontal number line labeled x_1 and a single point (the origin dot) marking where the linear threshold function crosses zero, representing a hyperplane as a point in 1D. Panel b) shows a two-dimensional input space with axes x_1 and x_2 and two colored lines passing through the origin: a vertical teal line and a horizontal orange-terracotta line, each representing a separate hyperplane boundary that divides the 2D plane into two half-spaces. Panel c) shows a three-dimensional input space with axes x_1, x_2, and x_3, rendered as a perspective cube with a light gray front face and teal side face, where the flat face of the cube represents a plane slicing through 3D space — the hyperplane in 3D. The figure demonstrates how the linear pre-activation of a neuron defines a hyperplane that separates input space into two regions, with the dimensionality of the hyperplane being one less than the input dimensionality.
authoredInteractions:
- Slider for weight w: tilt the orientation of a selected hyperplane by adjusting one weight component and watch the shaded positive/negative classification regions update in the plot
- Drag an input point (x1, x2, x3): move the point through the 3D feature space and show which side of each neuron's hyperplane it falls on, with the final output class updating to reflect the combined decisions

interactions.label: Input dimension
interactions.teaches: A neuron's zero set is always one dimension lower than the input space: a point in 1D, a line in 2D, and a plane in 3D
Focusing on one neuron makes clear that changing that neuron's weights rotates only its own decision boundary while the other neurons' boundaries stay fixed

interactions.label: Selected weight component
interactions.teaches: Changing a single weight component tilts the selected hyperplane because the weight vector is the hyperplane normal
Moving the input point through feature space shows that each neuron records which side of its hyperplane the point lies on, and the final class changes when the combined side pattern changes

demo_steps.title: 1D hyperplane is a point
demo_steps.narration: In one input dimension, the neuron's threshold w_1 x_1 + b = 0 is just a point on the x_1 axis. The black input point is classified by whether it lies to the left or right of that point.

demo_steps.title: 2D hyperplanes are lines
demo_steps.narration: In two dimensions, each neuron boundary becomes a line through the plane. Drag the input point across a colored line to see that neuron's sign flip.

demo_steps.title: Tilt one neuron's boundary
demo_steps.narration: With the teal hyperplane selected, increasing the weight component rotates its line or plane while the orange and gray boundaries remain fixed. The positive and negative shaded regions rotate with it.

demo_steps.title: 3D hyperplanes are planes
demo_steps.narration: In three dimensions, the decision boundaries are planes slicing feature space. The input point's side relative to each plane forms the hidden-layer decision pattern used for the final class.

interactionPlan.geometry_notes: Use an axonometric/isometric scene matching the source: x1 is horizontal screen-right, x2 is vertical screen-up, and x3 recedes diagonally down-left. World scale: axes span about -3 to +3 in each coordinate. Origin at (0,0,0) with a black sphere radius 0.07. 1D view: x1 axis length 6, teal marker is a thin rectangular slab centered at x1=0, about 0.08 wide by 0.9 high in screen space, color #9bd8d4 at about 0.75 opacity. 2D view: x1 and x2 axes length 6; teal line initially x1=0, length 5.2, stroke width visually thick, color #9bd8d4; orange line initially x2=0, length 5.2, color #d4835f. 3D view: draw a reference cube/domain from x,y,z = -2.2 to +2.2, mostly invisible except through translucent hyperplane quads. Teal plane initially x1=0, vertical, spanning x2 and x3, color #9bd8d4 with opacity 0.65. Orange plane initially x2=0, horizontal/slanted in the source view, spanning x1 and x3, color #d4835f with opacity 0.75. Gray plane initially x3=0, vertical/back rectangular plane, color #c6ced0 with opacity 0.7. The original source planes all pass through the origin, so use b=0 by default. Selected plane equation is w_j^T x + b_j = 0. Base normals: teal w=(1,0,0), orange w=(0,1,0), gray w=(0,0,1). The weightComponent slider adds a cross-component to the selected normal: teal becomes (1, alpha, 0), orange becomes (alpha, 1, 0), gray becomes (alpha, 0, 1), with alpha from the slider. Positive side is where w_j^T x + b_j > 0; negative side is where it is < 0. Draggable input point default at approximately (0.8,0.7,0.6), black sphere radius 0.09. Show dashed black guide lines from the point toward the origin/reference planes, like the dashed diagonal and vertical guides in panel c. Use math italic labels x_1, x_2, x_3 placed just beyond positive axis arrowheads. Final output can be a simple shallow-network combination: h_j = 1[w_j^T x + b_j > 0], class = +1 if h_teal + h_orange + h_gray >= 2 else -1; in 1D and 2D use only the visible neurons in the majority count.
interactionPlan.notes: Because the source is a multi-panel figure, show only one dimension view at a time through the inputDimension toggle rather than laying out all panels simultaneously. Fade/transition between 1D, 2D, and 3D views while preserving axis orientation. Use transparent double-sided PlaneGeometry clipped to the cubic domain for hyperplanes; recompute the selected plane vertices from the current normal and b=0 when weightComponent changes. For half-space shading, add subtle translucent overlays or colored halos on the selected plane's positive and negative sides, but keep them light enough that the source-like colored planes remain recognizable. Dragging should update the point coordinates, dashed guides, each neuron sign badge, and the final output class continuously.

discrepancies: In panel c, the gray plane is offset behind the origin instead of clearly passing through the origin with the x1 and x2 axes as in the source.
Panel c plane proportions and overlaps are noticeably different: the orange plane is too front-centered and dominant, while the teal and gray planes do not match the source overhangs and extents.
The black origin dot in panel c is much less prominent and is partly obscured by the translucent planes, whereas it is a clear central marker in the source.
The x3 axis and label in panel c are less clearly aligned with the diagonal down-left axis from the source.
Overall panel c is compressed relative to panels a and b and loses some of the distinctive large 3D composition of the reference.
evaluation.notes: The generated figure is recognizable and includes all three panels with useful interactions, but panel c has the most important spatial and proportional mismatches.
action_items: Reposition the gray plane in panel c so it clearly passes through the origin and aligns with the x1-x2 plane from the source.
Resize and reshape the three panel c planes to better match the reference overhangs, overlaps, and relative extents.
Increase the visibility of the panel c origin dot and ensure axes render cleanly above the translucent planes.
Move the x3 label and axis arrow so the diagonal down-left direction is more visually faithful to the source.
plan_action_items: Clarify that panel c should depict the three coordinate hyperplanes intersecting at the origin, not an offset background gray sheet.

feedback.rationale: Scores are uniformly high with only Scale-Wrong issues in panel c, and the remaining discrepancies are proportional/positioning refinements rather than plan or concept failures.
